claims.text: The structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoparticles over 473–1923 K is governed by the degree of local lattice-strain uniformity.
Uniformly distributed lattice distortion minimizes diffusion pathways needed for phase separation or elemental segregation.
Minimizing these diffusion pathways maintains a metastable solid solution during extreme thermal cycling.
The relevant initial state is nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
Local lattice distortion and its associated atomic-scale diffusion activation barriers are the structural mediator of stability.
Uniform lattice distortions increase diffusion barriers.
Increased diffusion barriers suppress atomic mobility.
Suppressed atomic mobility prevents phase separation and elemental segregation at elevated temperatures.
A nonuniform strain distribution facilitates diffusion pathways and thereby permits structural and chemical demixing.
Nanoparticles with more uniform lattice strain will retain a single-phase solid-solution structure and homogeneous elemental distribution after thermal exposure.
Retention of structural and chemical homogeneity will preserve catalytic and thermoelectric functionality.
Nanoparticles with heterogeneous lattice distortions will exhibit phase separation and property degradation.
The prediction is expected to hold for controlled thermal ramp rates and dwell times that avoid excessively rapid heating and prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Kinetic trapping or interfacial-energy effects may also contribute to stability.
A lack of correlation between strain uniformity and single-phase retention would falsify the hypothesis.
